summary: Cape d'Or on the Bay of Fundy: a fog whistle from 1874 or 1875, a light from 1922 in a tower moved from Eatonville, and a concrete tower from 1965.

structures.note: Steam fog whistle in operation December 1874 (Lighthouse Friends quoting the Department); 1875 per the Nova Scotia society; 1874 per the local history.

structures.type: square concrete tower with red top, joined to fog signal building
structures.note: Coast Guard list: white square tower with red top, connected to white building.

structures.type: square wooden tower, moved from Eatonville
structures.note: Built at Eatonville (Department, year ended 31 March 1909; local history gives 1908); moved to Cape d'Or in the year ended 31 March 1923; 5th-order lens. Stood on a red wooden trestle.

access.note: Grounds open, tower closed (Lighthouse Friends). Cape d'Or Road, a dirt road, runs 5.6 km from Route 209 just west of Advocate Harbour; a short hike down and up a steep road leads from the parking area to the light.

stay.note: Four rooms in one of the two keepers' houses (Lighthouse Friends). The other house is a restaurant. Operated by a private operator.

facts.agency: Owner per the Nova Scotia Lighthouse Preservation Society and the local history: Municipality of the County of Cumberland. Lighthouse Friends says the Canadian Coast Guard owns it. Not resolved.

events.note: Steam fog whistle placed in operation December 1874 (Lighthouse Friends). The Nova Scotia society gives 1875; the local history gives 1874.
Storm swept away the coal tramway and destroyed the station's boat (Lighthouse Friends); the local history says the storm destroyed the tramway.
Fog-alarm signal changed to one blast of six seconds every minute (report for year ended 31 March 1908).
Small wooden lighthouse erected at Eatonville: the Department's report for the year ended 31 March 1909 records the erection; Lighthouse Friends and the local history give 1908. Not at Cape d'Or.

First light at Cape d'Or, fifth-order lens in a tower moved from Eatonville (Lighthouse Friends, Nova Scotia society and local history give 1922; Department report of the year ended 31 March 1923 records the move). The Nova Scotia society says the tower is believed to have come by water from Apple River instead; the Department and the local history name Eatonville.
Old Eatonville light tower removed to Cape d'Or.
Present concrete tower built (Lighthouse Friends, Nova Scotia society and local history). The Nova Scotia society puts the replacement of the 1922 tower at 1966 to 1970.
Keepers' houses (built 1958/59) left vacant after 1989, then leased in 1995 by the Advocate District Development Association through the County of Cumberland and converted into a tearoom and hostel.

keepers.note: Local history and Lighthouse Friends agree (1939-1958). The Nova Scotia society quotes Walter Barteaux, who grew up at the cape, recalling that his father kept the light 19 years from 1939. The society does not name the father; the years and surname match this entry, but no source links them in so many words.

keepers.name: Ernie Morris
keepers.note: Local history 1985-89; the Nova Scotia society calls him the last keeper.

corrections.why: The 1874 date is the steam fog whistle, not a light. The first light at Cape d'Or was the tower moved from Eatonville, lit in 1922 (Lighthouse Friends, Nova Scotia society, local history). The Department's report for the year ended 31 March 1923 records the move and the fifth-order lens.

corrections.current: Concrete tower 10.7 m, built date missing
corrections.proposed: Concrete tower built 1965 (fog signal building with light tower; 10.7 m per the Coast Guard list)
corrections.why: The record's tower is the 1965 concrete structure. Lighthouse Friends describes a one-story fog signal building with a light tower rising from one corner.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Coast Guard list gives LFl W 6s, which settles the record's conflict with the Wikidata value (Fl W 9s). The Nova Scotia society's 1992 description (flashing white 7.5 s) is older and not used.
The Coast Guard list gives 20.3 m; the Nova Scotia society gives 79 ft (about 24 m). The Coast Guard figure is used as the official current value.

resolved_conflicts.field: built (Eatonville tower, origin of the Cape d'Or light)
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Department's report for the year ended 31 March 1909 records the Eatonville erection; Lighthouse Friends and the local history give 1908. The story gives both. Origin: the Department (FY1923) and the local history say Eatonville; the Nova Scotia society says the tower is believed to have come by water from Apple River. The story states the society's view and does not adopt it.

notes_for_editor: Checked 2026-10-28 against the page images and the sources. Fog whistle start: December 1874 (Lighthouse Friends, quoting the Department), 1874 (local history), 1875 (Nova Scotia society). Not resolved; the story says 1874 or 1875. The 1874-75 Department report is not in the corpus, so the Lighthouse Friends quotation stands as second-hand, and the story says so. Light date: 1922 (three secondary sources), with the Department's FY1923 report (scan p. 106, printed p. 99) as the primary record of the move. The Nova Scotia society's belief that the tower came by water from Apple River is stated in the story and not adopted. The Eatonville erection: the Department's FY1909 report (scan p. 61, printed p. 54) gives the year ended 31 March 1909; Lighthouse Friends and the local history say 1908; the story gives both. The 1908 fog-alarm change is in the year ended 31 March 1908 (scan p. 75, printed p. 66), and the story says so. Keepers: the Dewis date (13 April 1898) and the 'engineer' label (1903 report) were matched by row and checked on the page images (1909 table scan p. 166, printed p. 159; 1903 list scan p. 230, printed p. 217). Phil Morris and Malcome McLeod disagree between Lighthouse Friends and the local history; both are in the roster with the disagreement noted. The McAleese appointment date of 30 Oct 1913 appears in a 1916 table, but the station is not clear from the column; not used. Walter Barteaux is quoted from the Nova Scotia society page; the society does not name his father, so the story does not name him either and notes the years without making the link. Owner: County of Cumberland (Nova Scotia society, local history) against Canadian Coast Guard (Lighthouse Friends); the record says county; left for the editor. The record's 'stay: inn' is replaced by the guesthouse description. The operator is named in Lighthouse Friends but not in the story. Chronicling America searched once for Cape d'Or; the phrase search returned unrelated pages and nothing was used. No wreck or rescue tied to the cape was found in the corpus or the sources read. The Dec 1874 whistle machinery figures are Lighthouse Friends' quotes from the report. The Walter Barteaux recollection is quoted on the Nova Scotia society page (the page does not say how it was gathered); the story paraphrases it. The story now says the tide rip and low, green cape come from the Nova Scotia society only.
